source_text:
εἶτα κατερᾶται εἰς ἀγγεῖα, ζεστῷ ὕδατι ἐπὶ
πλεῖστον βραχεὶς καὶ ἀναληφθεὶς κυρτίσιν ἐξιποῦται. Ἔνιοι δὲ κόψαντες καὶ ὕδατι
φυράσαντες ἐν κριβάνοις ἀποτίθενται ἔστ' ἂν ζεσθῇ, οὕτως τε ἐξιποῦσιν. Τὸ δὲ δὴ
τερμίνθινον ὁμοίως τῷ σχινίνῳ σκευάζεται. Ἄλλοι δὲ κόψαντες ἐμβάλλουσιν εἰς
χύτρας ἐχούσας ὀλίγον ὑπερέχον ὕδωρ, εἶθ' ἑψοῦσιν καὶ τὸ ἐπιπλέον ἐλαιῶδες
ἐκλέγουσιν· (ἔλαιον χρηστὸν ἀποβαίνει εἰς τὸν πυθμένα τοῦ κεραμίου, καθέντος
ἀνήθου χλωροῦ καὶ ἁλός). Ἔλαιον δὲ μέλαν καὶ ῥυπαρὸν ὧδε λαμπρυνεῖς· λίτρου
λίτραν μίαν ὀπτήσας, κόψας, σήσας, βάλε εἰς τὸ κεράμιον. Ἐὰν δὲ καὶ θέλῃς οἷον
ὀμφάκινον αὐτὸ ποιῆσαι, φλοιὸν ἐλαίας ἀγρίας καὶ φύλλα κόψας, ποίει μάζαν καὶ
σταθμῷ λίτραν βάλε εἰς κεράμιον. Ἐὰν δὲ ὃ πρῶτον εἶπον τὸ Ἰβηρικὸν ὃ δὴ
«Σπάνον» ὀνομάζομεν ἐθελήσῃς ποιῆσαι, εἰς Σιδητικὸν ἔλαιον πάνυ διαυγὲς
ἀγριελαίας φύλλα συγκόψας βάλε ὀθόνῃ συμμέτρῳ ἀποδήσας καὶ ἀποκρεμάσας ἔα
βρέχεσθαι ὅσας θέλεις ἡμέρας· καὶ οὕτως τὴν Ἰβηρικὴν ποιότητα προσκτήσεται. Ἰάσαιο δ' ἂν θολερὸν ἔλαιον ἐγχέας εἰς πλατύστομον ἀγγεῖον καὶ ἐν σταθερῷ ἡλίῳ
ἀποθέμενος, ἁλῶν τε ἐπιπάσσων τῶν φρυκτῶν αὐτάρκως, ἐπὶ τὸ ἀναθερμαίνεσθαι· ὁπόταν δὲ καταστῇ, μέταιρε εἰς ἀγγεῖα. Τὸ δὲ δυσῶδες οὕτως· ἐλαίας χλωρᾶς
συγκόψας δίχα τῶν πυρήνων ὅσον ἡμιχοίνικα ἔμβαλε εἰς τὸν μετρητήν· ἀποθέμενος
δ' ἐν ἡλίῳ καὶ πυρώσας ἱκανῶς, εἶτ' ἐξελὼν τὸ ἐμβληθέν, μετέρασον εἰς ἀγγεῖα
πλείονα. Κἀκ στῆρος δὲ μοσχείου γένοιτο ἂν ἔλαιον καὶ ἄνοσμον ἔλαιον· κολυμβάδων ζωμοῦ χοᾶς <...> ἔμβαλε εἰς χαλκεῖον καὶ τοῦ στῆρος ἐν θαλλίδι
[σπυρίδι] μνᾶς ιʹ· ἐχέτω δὲ βάρος πρὸς τὸ μὴ ἐπιπολάζειν, ἐγκείμενον λίθον, καὶ
ὑπόκαιε μαλακῷ πυρί· τὸ δὲ ἀναζέον ἀφαιρῶν, ὑπὸ χεῖρα εἰς κεράμιον ἐλαιηρὸν
νεοκένωτον βάλε· ἐκτακέντος δὲ τοῦ στῆρος τὸ ὑπόλοιπον ἠθμῷ διυλίσας ἐπέμβαλε
τῷ ἀγγείῳ, καὶ αὐτὸ διαλαβὼν ἔασον ἐφ' ἡμέρας κʹ· εἶτα τότε χρῶ. Ἀλλὰ καὶ γάρος
ἐξ ἅλμης ἀκράτου μέρους ἑνὸς καὶ δύο οἴνου τοῦ γλυκέος. Ἀπὸ Λυδίας ὁ σπουδαῖος
γίνεται· ὁ δὲ «σόκκιος» ὀνομαζόμενος ὃν μᾶλλον ἁπάντων γάρων ἐπαινοῦσι.
pass_a_gloss: then it-is-poured-down into vessels, with-boiling water upon longest having-been-soaked and having-been-taken-up with-wicker-baskets it-is-squeezed-out. Some but having-chopped and with-water having-mixed in ovens they-set-away until it-be-boiled, thus both they-squeeze-out. The but then terebinth-oil likewise to-the mastic-oil is-prepared. Others but having-chopped they-throw into pots having little standing-above water, then they-boil and the floating-on-top oily they-pick-off; (oil good comes-off into the bottom of-the jar, having-been-let-down of-dill green and of-salt). Oil but black and dirty thus you-will-brighten: of-nitre litra one having-roasted, having-chopped, having-sifted, throw into the jar. If but also you-want like omphacinum it to-make, bark of-olive wild and leaves having-chopped, make a-mass and by-weight litra throw into jar. If but what first I-said the Iberian which indeed "Spanum" we-name you-should-want to-make, into Sidetic oil very clear of-wild-olive leaves having-chopped-together throw with-linen proportionate having-bound and having-hung let soak as-many you-want days; and thus the Iberian quality it-will-acquire. You-would-heal but turbid oil having-poured into wide-mouth vessel and in steady sun having-set-away, of-salts both sprinkling of-the roasted sufficiently, upon the to-be-rewarmed; whenever but it-has-settled, transfer into vessels. The but foul-smelling thus: of-olive green having-chopped-together without the pits as-much-as half-choenix throw into the metretes; having-set-away but in sun and having-heated enough, then having-taken-out the having-been-thrown-in, transfer into vessels more. And-from suet but of-calf could-come even oil and odorless oil; of-pickled-olives of-brine choes <lacuna> throw into bronze-kettle and of-the suet in a-basket [in a-creel] minas 10; let-it-have but weight toward the not to-float, laid-in a-stone, and fire-under with-soft fire; the but boiling-up taking-off, under hand into jar oil newly-emptied throw; having-been-melted but of-the suet the remainder with-strainer having-filtered throw-on to-the vessel, and it having-taken-aside let upon days 20; then then use. But also garum from of-brine unmixed of-part one and two of-wine the sweet. From Lydia the serious comes; the but "soccius" being-named which more of-all garums they-praise.
pass_b_english: Then it is poured down into vessels; soaked the longest time in boiling water and taken up, it is squeezed out with wicker baskets. Some, having chopped and mixed with water, set them in ovens until it is boiled, and thus squeeze them out. The terebinth-oil is prepared likewise to the mastic. Others, having chopped, throw them into pots that have a little water standing above, then boil and pick off the oily that floats on top (good oil comes off to the bottom of the jar, green dill and salt having been let down).

Black and dirty oil you will brighten thus: roast one litra of nitre, chop it, sift it, throw it into the jar. If you also want to make it like omphacinum, chop bark of wild olive and leaves, make a mass, and by weight throw a litra into a jar. If you want to make the Iberian I first said, which we name "Spanum," throw chopped wild-olive leaves into very clear Sidetic oil, having bound them in a proportionate linen and hung them, and let them soak as many days as you want; and thus it will acquire the Iberian quality.

You would heal turbid oil by pouring it into a wide-mouth vessel and setting it in steady sun, and sprinkling roasted salts sufficiently, toward the rewarming; whenever it has settled, transfer it into vessels. The foul-smelling thus: chop green olive without the pits, as much as a half-choenix, throw it into the metretes; set it in the sun and heat it enough, then take out what was thrown in and transfer into more vessels.

And from calf suet oil could come, even odorless oil: choes of pickled-olive brine — the measure is lost in the lock — throw into a bronze kettle, and of the suet in a basket ten minas; let it have a weight toward not floating, a stone laid in, and fire underneath with a soft fire. Taking off what boils up, throw it at once into a newly-emptied oil-jar; and of the suet having melted, filter the remainder with a strainer and throw it onto the vessel, and having taken it aside let it for twenty days; then use it. But also garum from one part of unmixed brine and two of the sweet wine. The serious one comes from Lydia; and the one named "soccius," which they praise more than all garums.

choices.english: it is squeezed out with wicker baskets
choices.why: κύρτη is a wicker weel/basket; ἐξιπόω is to press the oil out.
